name: Francois Pienaar
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Springbok debut on 26 June 1993 at age 26, captaining South Africa against France in Durban — a rare instance of debuting as national team captain.
early_history_summary: Born into a working-class Afrikaner family in Vereeniging, Pienaar won an athletic scholarship to Rand Afrikaans University to study law. He debuted for Transvaal province in 1989 at age 22 and captained the side to multiple titles before being named Springbok captain on his international debut in 1993.
family_context_summary: Born into a working-class Afrikaner family in Vereeniging, Transvaal; eldest of four boys. Father worked in a steelworks family context.
primary_early_advantage_tags: South Africa rugby culture, athletic scholarship, working-class drive
evidence_summary: Pienaar grew up in a working-class Afrikaner family in Vereeniging, immersed in South Africa's rugby-dominant culture. He won an athletic scholarship to RAU where he studied law and played rugby, debuting for Transvaal in 1989 at age 22. By 1993 he was named Springbok captain on his international debut at age 26, a remarkably fast rise. His physical stature (1.91m, 108kg) and natural leadership were key assets. No family rugby background or financial privilege is documented.
starting_point: Born into a working-class Afrikaner family in Vereeniging, South Africa; eldest of four boys; father worked in industry.
current_position: Director at Saracens (Premiership rugby club); part of a consortium that took over the club in 2022; married to Nerine Winter with two sons.

trajectory.event: Debuted for Transvaal provincial rugby team, beginning a 100-cap career with 89 as captain.
Made Springbok debut as national captain against France in Durban, a rare instance of captaining on debut.
Named International Player of the Year by Rugby World magazine; led Transvaal to Currie Cup retention.
Captained South Africa to Rugby World Cup victory on home soil, famously received by Nelson Mandela in a Springbok jersey.
Joined English club Saracens, playing until 2000 and later coaching there.
Became a director at Saracens as part of a consortium takeover of the Premiership club.

name: Alfred Aho
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; he completed his PhD at Princeton in 1967 at age 26 and joined Bell Labs, but his notable contributions (AWK, Aho-Corasick algorithm, Dragon Book) all came in the 1970s-80s.

name: Thomas Wassberg
milestone_by_age_26: Won the unofficial overall World Cup title in 1977 at age 21, with podium finishes in Lapland World Cup competitions, marking his breakthrough as an elite senior international skier.
early_history_summary: Born in Lennartsfors near Årjäng, Sweden, Wassberg began skiing as a child; his father took him to Holmenkollen in Oslo before he started school. He attended the ski gymnasium in Järpen in 1972 at age 16, served in the military sports platoon in Östersund, and won junior European gold in 1974. His senior breakthrough came in 1977 at age 21 with World Cup podiums and the unofficial overall World Cup title.
family_context_summary: Born in the small village of Lennartsfors near Årjäng in western Sweden, close to the Norwegian border. His father Olle took him to Holmenkollen ski races as a young boy, sparking his interest in the sport.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father introduced him to competitive skiing culture by taking him to Holmenkollen races before school age, but no evidence of professional skiing background in the family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Ski gymnasium Järpen, military sports platoon, Swedish national team, Nordic skiing culture, Holmenkollen exposure
evidence_summary: Wassberg grew up in a small Swedish village near the Norwegian border, immersed in Nordic skiing culture from childhood. His father took him to Holmenkollen races before he started school. At 16 he entered Sweden's first ski gymnasium in Järpen (1972), then served in the military sports platoon at I5 Östersund, creating an elite training pipeline. He won junior European gold in 1974 and became Sweden's youngest Olympic skier in 1976 at age 20. His senior breakthrough came in 1977 at age 21 with World Cup podiums and the unofficial overall World Cup title. Teammates noted his unusual physical recovery — he looked fresh when others were exhausted.
starting_point: Born in the small village of Lennartsfors near Årjäng, Sweden, close to the Norwegian border; father Olle introduced him to skiing culture by taking him to Holmenkollen races as a boy.
current_position: Retired from competitive skiing; lives in Åsarna, Sweden; works as a forester and serves as chairman and track manager for Åsarna IK; married to Ulrike Wieser.

trajectory.event: Won junior European Championship gold in cross-country skiing.
Became Sweden's youngest ever Olympic cross-country skier at the Innsbruck Winter Olympics, finishing 15th in the 15km.
Achieved senior breakthrough with World Cup podiums in Lapland and won the unofficial overall World Cup title.
Won Olympic gold in the 15km at Lake Placid, beating Juha Mieto by one hundredth of a second; also won the Holmenkollen medal.
Won World Championship gold in the 50km at Holmenkollen, Oslo.
Won two Olympic gold medals at Sarajevo: the 50km individual and the 4x10km relay.
Dominated the World Championships in Oberstdorf with two golds (30km, relay) and two silvers (15km, 50km).
Won his fourth Olympic gold in the 4x10km relay at Calgary and served as Sweden's Olympic flag bearer.

name: Mariano Rivera
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Major League Baseball debut on May 23, 1995 for the New York Yankees at age 25, reaching the highest level of professional baseball.
early_history_summary: Raised in the modest Panamanian fishing village of Puerto Caimito, Rivera did not pitch seriously until 1989 when a Yankees scout saw him. He was signed for a $3,000 bonus in February 1990 at age 20 and worked through the minor leagues for five years, including overcoming a 1992 arm injury, before his fastball velocity jumped and he earned a promotion to the majors in 1995.
family_context_summary: Raised in the modest fishing village of Puerto Caimito, Panama, with limited resources. His father was a fisherman. Rivera worked on his father's boat as a youth before being discovered by baseball scouts.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; family had no baseball background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Poverty in Panama, $3000 signing bonus, Yankees scout discovery, arm injury recovery, velocity jump
evidence_summary: Rivera grew up in a poor fishing village in Panama with no baseball infrastructure or family background in the sport. He was signed by the Yankees for just $3,000 in 1990 at age 20 after scout Herb Raybourn spotted him. He spent five years in the minor leagues, surviving a 1992 arm injury that left him unprotected in the expansion draft. His fastball velocity jumped from 91 to 96 mph at Triple-A Columbus in 1995, earning his MLB debut at age 25. His natural arm talent and later development of the devastating cut fastball propelled him to become the greatest closer in baseball history.
starting_point: Raised in the modest fishing village of Puerto Caimito, Panama; father was a fisherman; Rivera worked on his father's boat as a youth with limited resources and no baseball infrastructure.
current_position: Retired from MLB (2013); inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2019 as the first unanimous selection in history; resides in Panama and the United States; net worth estimated at ~$90 million.

trajectory.event: Signed by the New York Yankees as an amateur free agent for a $3,000 bonus after being scouted in Panama.
Made MLB debut on May 23 as a starting pitcher for the Yankees, later converting to relief.
Breakthrough season as primary setup man for closer John Wetteland; Yankees won the World Series.
Became the Yankees' full-time closer, beginning his path to becoming the greatest closer in MLB history.
Won World Series MVP Award and led the major leagues in saves; Yankees won their third World Series in four years.
Retired as the all-time saves leader (652) with a career ERA of 2.21 over 19 seasons.
Inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame as the first ever unanimous selection, appearing on all 425 ballots.

name: René Burri
milestone_by_age_26: His first major photo reportage 'Touch of Music for the Deaf' was published in Life magazine in 1955 at age 22, and he became an associate of Magnum Photos the same year, launching his career at one of the world's most prestigious photo agencies.
early_history_summary: Born in Zurich to a cook father and a mother from a farming family, Burri photographed Winston Churchill at age 13 using his father's camera. He studied photography at the Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich from 1949 to 1953 under Hans Finsler and Johannes Itten, then worked as a documentary filmmaker and cameraman for Disney before his breakthrough photo essay was published in Life in 1955.
family_context_summary: Born in Zurich, Switzerland; father was a cook and mother came from a family of farmers. He described his youth as modest, quiet, and sheltered. His father owned a camera which Burri used to photograph Churchill at age 13.
parent_family_domain_summary: No professional photography background in the family, but his father owned a camera that Burri used from a young age, and his parents supported his art education.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich, Hans Finsler mentor, Werner Bischof Magnum connection, Life magazine publication, golden age of photojournalism
evidence_summary: Burri grew up in modest circumstances in Zurich, son of a cook and a farmer's daughter. He showed early talent by photographing Churchill at 13 with his father's camera. He received formal photography training at the prestigious Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich (1949-53) under Hans Finsler and Johannes Itten, then worked as a cameraman for Disney. His breakthrough came in 1955 at age 22 when his photo essay 'Touch of Music for the Deaf' was published in Life magazine and he became a Magnum associate through Werner Bischof's connection. He became a full Magnum member in 1959 at age 26, with Cartier-Bresson as his mentor. He was well-positioned in the golden age of photo-magazines.
starting_point: Born in Zurich, Switzerland to a cook father and a mother from a farming family; modest, quiet upbringing; used his father's camera to photograph Winston Churchill at age 13.
current_position: Died on 20 October 2014 in Zurich at age 81 from cancer; final role: renowned Swiss photographer and longtime member of Magnum Photos.

trajectory.event: Photographed Winston Churchill in Zurich using his father's camera, an early display of photographic talent.
Completed photography degree at the Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich under Hans Finsler and Johannes Itten.
Published first major photo reportage 'Touch of Music for the Deaf' in Life magazine; became a Magnum Photos associate through Werner Bischof.
Became a full member of Magnum Photos, with Henri Cartier-Bresson as his mentor.
Photographed Che Guevara in Cuba, producing iconic images of the revolutionary smoking a cigar.
Elected chair of Magnum France, cementing his leadership role in the legendary photo agency.
Died of cancer on 20 October 2014 in Zurich.
